own_scenes.desc: El funk volvió a la madre África. Manu Dibango llevó la música africana a la radio negra con «Soul Makossa» (1972), que inspiró «Jungle Boogie» de Kool & the Gang. Fela Anikulapo Kuti metió el filo de James Brown en su afrobeat, sobre todo tras conocerlo en 1970: guitarra rítmica cortante, piezas de veinte minutos y una política durísima («music is the weapon») que le costó el asalto a su casa en 1977. Brown lo llamó «el James Brown africano».

notes.chapter: Cap. 14: United Funk: The Shining Star
notes.text: Masekela, Olatunji, Osibisa, Cymande o Mongo Santamaría tenían público negro; «Soul Makossa» formalizó el estilo y empujó a Kool & the Gang a grabar «Funky Stuff» y «Jungle Boogie». La sección de percusión africana se volvió imprescindible en el funk: Santana y Hendrix en Woodstock, los Temptations de Whitfield, «The Ghetto», «Inner City Blues», «Pusherman», «Hollywood Swinging», «Fire».

influences.name: James Brown, el Padrino del Soul

refs.q: Multifaceted saxophonist Manu Dibango was one of the first Africans to incorporate The Funk into his sound
refs.para: New Orleans music opened the vast rhythmic chasm of African music for practitioners of The Funk. It should come as no surprise, then, that across the Atlantic Ocean, from South Africa to Morocco, African musicians with their ears to the West heard The Funk and internalized it as their own. Multifaceted saxophonist Manu Dibango was one of the first Africans to incorporate The Funk into his sound, recording the influential “Soul Makossa” in 1972. A fast-paced club scorcher with smart, African congas, a phased-out, funky rhythm guitar, and Dibango’s percussive ad-libs on top, “Soul Makossa” kicked The Funk and brought African music to black radio. (His work was the inspiration for Kool & the Gang’s smash hit “Jungle Boogie” in 1973.) With a groove that ranged from High Life—electrified traditional rhythms—to the wicked grooves of James Brown funk, Dibango became the ambassador to the African music sound for many American soul music fans.
refs.chapter: Cap. 6: La revolución rítmica: Tighten Up

refs.q: As far as The Funk was concerned, an African percussion section was an essential ingredient, musically speaking.
refs.para: As far as The Funk was concerned, an African percussion section was an essential ingredient, musically speaking. From the earliest days of psychedelic black rock—Santana and Hendrix’s six-piece Band of Gypsys at Woodstock in 1969—to the extended Norman Whitfield sessions on Temptations’ albums at the otherwise stuffy Motown Records, Africa had come home to the heart of black music. Rich, percussion-filled breakdowns can be heard on many of the early seventies soul-funk standards such as Donny Hathaway’s “The Ghetto” (studio and live versions), Marvin Gaye’s “Inner City Blues,” Curtis Mayfield’s “Pusherman,” Kool & the Gang’s “Hollywood Swinging,” and the Ohio Players’ “Fire.”

podcast.title: International Expansion via YouTube
podcast.body: Afrobeat has successfully expanded internationally, largely due to YouTube's global accessibility and monetization model. This demonstrates how the platform has flattened everything, removing geographic barriers and allowing diverse musical genres to thrive worldwide. "Afrobeat has gone international."
